Chapter 6. The People Who Stay, the People Who Go: Farewells and Enduring Ties.
You know, there’s a moment on the farm when you can just feel that something’s changing. The air gets a little heavier, and suddenly, the days seem to slip by faster. Routines that once felt so familiar now have a bittersweet edge to them. And then, you start to notice—some faces that used to light up the mornings and fill the evenings with laughter are gone. Their absence echoes in the quiet spaces they leave behind.
There’s this one worker—one of the oldest on the farm. His hands have shaped these fields for decades. When he finally decides it’s time to return to his ancestral village, it’s not just another goodbye. You watch him move slowly, gathering his few belongings, pausing now and then to look out at the land he’s known almost his whole life. And the farm owner? She stands by, feeling that strange mix of gratitude and sadness. It’s almost like there’s a silent promise between them—that the land will remember him, even if people come and go.
Not everyone leaves the same way. A young woman, once a barefoot child darting between coffee rows, ties the knot and heads off to a distant town. Her mother wipes away a tear, but you can tell there’s pride in her eyes too. Then there are the Somali herders—always a bit restless—drifting away with the seasons, their camels trailing behind like long, gentle shadows. The Swahili traders? They show up less and less, chasing new chances somewhere else.
But not all goodbyes are forever. Some people stay. The elders who’ve seen the farm through both drought and harvest, the kids who now pick up the same chores their parents once did, and the owner herself—anchored by love and responsibility. The ties between those who stay and those who leave aren’t easy to break. Letters go back and forth, news travels slowly, and at night, memories get passed around the fire like treasured stories.
It’s in these moments that you realize—the farm isn’t just a patch of land. It’s a web of relationships, a living memory that stretches far beyond any fence or field. Most people don’t really see how deeply they’re tied to the places and people they leave behind. Here, though, every farewell is a gentle reminder that belonging is never simple, and it’s never really finished.
And here’s the thing: departures aren’t just about losing someone—they’re about new beginnings, too. Everyone who leaves takes a piece of the farm with them, weaving it into their own stories and dreams. And those who remain? They find new ways to keep the community strong, drawing comfort and strength from the land and from each other.
